problem: "provincial liberties" rendered as "the liberties of the States", narrowing the term to the defined term 'the States'; the source does not say States.
replacement: Some people in Europe have formed an opinion about the influence General Jackson may have on the affairs of his country, and those who have looked more closely into the matter find it highly exaggerated. We have been told that General Jackson has won a number of battles, that he is an energetic man, inclined by nature and by habit to use force, greedy for power, and a despot by temperament. All this may perhaps be true, but the conclusions drawn from it are badly mistaken. People have imagined that General Jackson is determined to establish a dictatorship in America, to introduce a military spirit, and to give the central authority a degree of influence that could not fail to endanger local liberties. But in America the time for such undertakings has not yet come, and neither has the age for men of this kind. If General Jackson had hoped to exercise his authority in this way, he would certainly have lost his political position and put his life at risk. He has accordingly not been so imprudent as to attempt anything of the kind.

problem: "forcible measures" softened to "strong measures"; the source means coercive measures against nullification.
replacement: Whenever the governments of the States come into conflict with that of the Union, the President is generally the first to doubt his own rights. He almost always goes further than the legislature, and when the extent of federal power is disputed, he takes sides, in a manner of speaking, against himself. He hides his official interests and suppresses his own natural inclinations. This is not because he is naturally weak or hostile to the Union. When the majority ruled against the claims of the supporters of nullification, he put himself at its head, stated the doctrines the nation held clearly and forcefully, and was the first to recommend forceful measures. But General Jackson seems to me, if I may use the American expressions, to be a Federalist by taste and a Republican by calculation.

problem: "as easily as no earlier President ever could" is illogical and garbled English for "with a facility which no former President ever enjoyed"; also "or at least" is a small addition.
replacement: General Jackson stoops to win the favor of the majority. But once he feels his popularity is secure, he sweeps aside every obstacle in pursuit of the goals the community approves of, or of those it does not view with a jealous eye. He is backed by a power his predecessors never knew, and he tramples on his personal enemies whenever they cross his path with an ease no earlier President ever enjoyed. He takes responsibility for measures that no one before him would have dared to attempt. He even treats the national representatives with a disdain that comes close to insult. He vetoes the laws of Congress, and he often does not bother to answer that powerful body. He is a favorite who sometimes treats his master roughly. The power of General Jackson is constantly growing, but that of the President is declining. In his hands the federal government is strong, but it will pass weakened to his successor.

problem: "common ... but not the second" sharpened to "plenty of the first but none of the second".
replacement: Experience shows that the two kinds of legislative instability are not necessarily linked, since they have appeared together or separately depending on the time and the circumstances. The first is common in the United States, but the second is not. The Americans change their laws often, yet the foundation of the Constitution is respected.
